acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis; baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment injury, prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → interstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia → isotonic crystalloid; congestion → loop diuretic; avoid reflex fluids in overloaded patients
Stop culprit nephrotoxins; renal-dose drugs; AIN persisting after withdrawal → consider glucocorticoids
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-respiratory-failure.name: Acute respiratory failure
acute-respiratory-failure.scope: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (type 1), hypercapnic respiratory failure (type 2), noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP), indications for invasive mechanical ventilation
acute-respiratory-failure.core: Acute inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation demands simultaneous cause treatment and escalating respiratory support, guided by work of breathing and airway safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, PE → oxygenation failure
COPD, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation, sedatives → ventilation failure; overlap common

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, hypoxemia, diaphoresis; hypercapnia may cause headache, somnolence, asterixis
★ **Exhaustion, declining consciousness, silent chest, paradoxical breathing** → impending respiratory arrest
Normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not exclude dangerous CO₂ retention

rows.label: Pathophys
items: V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment lowers PaO₂; shunt may resist oxygen alone
Inadequate alveolar ventilation raises PaCO₂; abrupt rise causes respiratory acidosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry + ABG** when severe distress, hypercapnia concern, or escalating support
Chest radiograph, ECG, bedside lung/cardiac ultrasound; infection/PE testing follows clinical context
Trend pH, gases, respiratory rate, mentation and effort; do not wait for an extreme number
Chronic compensated hypercapnia has elevated bicarbonate; pH decline identifies acute deterioration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen immediately**, treat cause; target SpO₂ 88–92% with CO₂-retention risk, usually 92–96% otherwise
Hypoxemic failure needing more than conventional oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula, close reassessment
★ Awake cooperative COPD + respiratory acidosis → **BiPAP**; cardiogenic edema → CPAP/BiPAP plus diuresis/nitrates
★ **Intubate** for airway failure, refractory hypoxemia, shock, arrest, exhaustion, or worsening despite noninvasive support
Avoid NIV with vomiting, unprotected airway, copious secretions, major facial trauma; reassess within 1–2 h

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrhythmia, multiorgan failure; delayed intubation worsens outcome
Positive pressure → hypotension/barotrauma; invasive ventilation → pneumonia and ventilator-induced lung injury
Ventilated ARDS: low tidal volume using predicted body weight, limited plateau pressure; prone if severe

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory vaccination, disease control, cautious sedatives, aspiration precautions
High-risk extubation patients may benefit from planned NIV rather than rescue after deterioration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metabolic acidosis: compensatory tachypnea with low CO₂
Panic hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis without sustained gas-exchange failure

adrenal-insufficiency.name: Adrenal insufficiency
adrenal-insufficiency.scope: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), secondary adrenal insufficiency, cosyntropin stimulation test, morning serum cortisol, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement, adrenal crisis
adrenal-insufficiency.core: Weight loss, fatigue, orthostasis, and hyponatremia, or unexplained pressor-resistant shock after illness or interruption of glucocorticoids.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: autoimmune destruction, TB, bilateral hemorrhage, metastases; associated autoimmune thyroid disease
★ Secondary: **prolonged glucocorticoids**, pituitary disease/surgery/apoplexy; abrupt withdrawal risks crisis
Crisis triggers: infection, trauma, surgery, missed replacement, vomiting

rows.label: Clues
items: Anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, weakness; hypoglycemia, eosinophilia
Crisis: fever, confusion, severe volume depletion; symptoms may worsen rapidly during intercurrent illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular catecholamine response and increases ADH
Primary gland failure removes mineralocorticoids; secondary disease retains renin–angiotensin-driven aldosterone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **8 AM cortisol + ACTH**; very low cortisol supports, clearly high values argue against insufficiency
★ Equivocal basal cortisol → **cosyntropin stimulation**; inadequate assay-specific peak confirms impaired reserve
Traditional stimulated cutoff ≈18 µg/dL; newer assays may use ≈14–15; interpret laboratory standard
Primary → 21-hydroxylase antibodies, selected adrenal CT; secondary → pituitary evaluation/MRI
Recent pituitary injury may initially show normal cosyntropin response; clinical suspicion still matters

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → draw blood if feasible, **IV hydrocortisone + isotonic saline**, dextrose for hypoglycemia
Do not wait for confirmatory results; treat precipitant and correct electrolytes carefully
Coexisting hypothyroidism → glucocorticoid replacement before levothyroxine to avoid decompensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → arrhythmia, circulatory collapse, death; chronic undertreatment → impaired function
Excess replacement → osteoporosis, diabetes, Cushingoid features

rows.label: Prevention
items: Stress-dose plan, emergency injectable hydrocortisone, medical alert ID; taper prolonged systemic steroids
Vomiting prevents absorption → parenteral replacement and urgent evaluation; teach sick-day plans to caregivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: SIADH: euvolemia, normal potassium and cortisol reserve
Sepsis: infection may coexist and trigger crisis
Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, cold intolerance, weight gain

rows: Low/inappropriately normal ACTH; potassium usually normal

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.scope: Acute appendicitis, clinical presentation, pediatric and pregnancy considerations, imaging (ultrasound, CT), surgical management
appendicitis.core: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, followed by anorexia and nausea, suggests appendiceal inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescents/young adults; luminal obstruction by lymphoid hyperplasia or fecalith
Older adults may have obstructing neoplasm; immunosuppression can blunt findings

rows.label: Clues
items: McBurney tenderness, guarding, fever; Rovsing, psoas, or obturator signs depend on position

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal obstruction → distention, venous congestion, bacterial invasion → ischemia/perforation
Visceral midgut pain precedes focal parietal peritoneal irritation

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; lactation and milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: painless postlactational mass; fat–fluid level on imaging
Abscess: focal tender erythematous fluctuant mass, sometimes fever; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → papilloma or malignancy evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound

Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Tx

Fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID; galactocele → aspiration if symptomatic
★ Abscess → ultrasound-guided drainage + **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**; MRSA risk → clindamycin

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation

Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients

★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Vestibular symptoms → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery

★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children

rows.label: Complications

burn-injuries.name: Burn injuries
burn-injuries.scope: Superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness burns, total body surface area (Rule of Nines), fluid resuscitation (Parkland), smoke inhalation and airway edema, carbon monoxide/cyanide toxicity
burn-injuries.core: Burn severity depends on depth, affected surface area, location, and inhalation injury; airway threats and hypovolemia take priority over wound care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Flames/scalds, electricity, chemicals; closed-space fires increase toxic inhalation risk
Older adults, children, impaired mobility/sensation; inconsistent injury history raises abuse concern

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hoarseness, stridor, oropharyngeal edema, soot** → threatened airway; skin burns may appear minor
CO: headache, confusion, syncope despite normal pulse oximetry
Cyanide: enclosed-fire exposure with cardiovascular collapse and severe lactic acidosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary leak → intravascular depletion and edema; swelling progresses after initial presentation
CO impairs oxygen transport; cyanide blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TBSA excludes superficial burns**; adult Rule of Nines: head/each arm 9%, each leg 18%
Anterior/posterior trunk 18% each, perineum 1%; own palm including fingers ≈1%; children → Lund-Browder
★ Inhalation/toxin concern → **ABG with co-oximetry**, lactate; normal PaO2 does not exclude CO
Electrical burn → ECG, CK, urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis; small surface injury may hide deep damage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway threat → **intubate**; burn center: full-thickness, ≥10% partial, critical-site, inhalation/electrical/chemical
CO → 100% oxygen; severe neurologic/cardiac toxicity or pregnancy → consider hyperbaric oxygen; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin
Lactated Ringer: classic **Parkland = 4 mL × kg × %TBSA** during first 24 hours
Half by 8 hours from injury, remainder over 16; ABA now starts adults at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA

rows.label: Complications
items: Shock, AKI, infection, contractures, compartment syndrome; overresuscitation worsens edema
Restrictive chest/limb eschar → escharotomy; true compartment syndrome → fasciotomy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Titrate fluids to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults; formula only starting estimate
Analgesia, cleaning, moist nonadherent dressings, tetanus; avoid routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis
★ **Stop exposure, remove jewelry, cool water**, prevent hypothermia; no ice
Smoke/CO detectors, safe water temperature, fire escape plan; early rehabilitation and range of motion

rows.label: Mimics
items: SJS/TEN: medication exposure, mucosal erosions, widespread epidermal detachment
Cellulitis: spreading warmth/erythema without immediate thermal exposure

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax**, contralateral weakness/numbness, or aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

cervical-radiculopathy.name: Cervical radiculopathy
cervical-radiculopathy.scope: C5-C8 radiculopathy, cervical disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, LMN arm and UMN leg signs, Spurling test, conservative management, MRI cervical spine, surgical decompression
cervical-radiculopathy.core: Neck pain radiating down one arm with a dermatomal sensory deficit and reduced corresponding reflex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Disc herniation in younger adults; osteophytes and foraminal narrowing with aging
Repetitive neck loading, smoking, prior cervical injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Spurling test**: extension, ipsilateral rotation, axial compression reproduce arm symptoms
Shoulder abduction may relieve root pain
★ **Myelopathy**: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, LMN arms plus UMN legs; late bladder dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Root compression → segmental weakness; central canal stenosis → spinal cord dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: Map strength, sensation, reflexes; examine gait, plantar responses, Hoffmann sign
★ **Cervical MRI**: myelopathy, progressive deficit, cancer/infection concern, or failed conservative care
EMG/nerve conduction studies if localization uncertain; sensory responses usually preserved in radiculopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **NSAIDs + physical therapy**, activity modification; most improve within weeks
Persistent disabling root pain → consider epidural steroid injection or surgical referral
Cord compression or progressive motor deficit → urgent spine evaluation for decompression
Avoid cervical manipulation with suspected myelopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent denervation and muscle atrophy; untreated cord compression → irreversible disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ergonomic adjustments, neck strengthening, smoking cessation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carpal tunnel: median hand symptoms, positive Phalen, no neck provocation
Rotator cuff disease: painful shoulder motion, preserved distal neurologic examination
Brachial plexopathy: multiple roots/nerves, abnormal sensory nerve responses

cervical-spine-injury.name: Cervical spine injury
cervical-spine-injury.scope: Whiplash, cervical strain, NEXUS criteria, Canadian C-spine rule, cervical fractures (odontoid, hangman, burst), atlantoaxial subluxation, spinal clearance
cervical-spine-injury.core: After trauma, protect the neck until a reliable low-risk examination or imaging excludes clinically significant cervical injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-energy collision, axial load, falls in older adults; osteoporosis
Rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome → atlantoaxial instability

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline tenderness, paresthesias, weakness; high cord injury may impair ventilation
Whiplash: acceleration-deceleration injury with muscular pain and stiffness, usually no neurologic deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fracture or ligament disruption → instability; secondary motion may injure spinal cord

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NEXUS**: alert; no intoxication, midline tenderness, focal deficit or distracting injury → clinical clearance
★ Canadian rule: **age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, or extremity paresthesias** → imaging
Low-risk features: simple rear-end collision, ambulatory, seated, delayed neck pain, or no midline tenderness
Low-risk feature present + active rotation 45° each way → clear; otherwise image
★ Imaging required → **CT cervical spine**; deficit or suspected ligament/cord injury → MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway with manual inline stabilization; immobilize suspected unstable injury and obtain spine consultation
Unstable fracture or cord compression → stabilization/decompression; avoid routine high-dose methylprednisolone
Uncomplicated strain after clearance: NSAIDs, early gentle mobilization and exercise; avoid prolonged soft-collar use
Negative high-quality CT usually permits collar removal without neurologic concern; discordant findings → spine consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Spinal cord injury, respiratory failure, neurogenic shock; immobilization → pressure injury and stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid axial loading during diving
★ **Do not force neck movement** in an unreliable examination or high-risk patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Muscular strain: paraspinal pain after dangerous injury excluded
Degenerative stenosis: chronic symptoms; may predispose to cord injury after minor trauma

table.title: Important patterns
rows: C2 dens; type II nonunion risk
Axial compression; retropulsion may injure cord
Axial load; transverse ligament injury may destabilize

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts increase pulmonary flow; longstanding vascular remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell → knee–chest position, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; irreversible Eisenmenger physiology → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ Hematemesis/melena, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia → **alarm evaluation**
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation; early satiety with recurrent vomiting → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years → upper endoscopy**; younger high-risk/alarm presentations assessed individually
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.scope: Diagnosis (beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone), unruptured ectopic pregnancy, medical management (methotrexate), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, surgical management
ectopic-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, usually tubal; early pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding requires localization and rupture assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior ectopic, PID/tubal damage, tubal surgery, infertility treatment, smoking
IUDs prevent pregnancy overall; pregnancy despite IUD has higher ectopic proportion; many cases lack risks

rows.label: Clues
items: Amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, spotting; cervical motion/adnexal tenderness nonspecific
★ **Syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritoneal signs, hypotension** → hemoperitoneum/rupture
Heterotopic pregnancy possible despite visualized intrauterine pregnancy, particularly after assisted reproduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired tubal transport → extrauterine trophoblastic implantation, invasion, hemorrhage
Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent DNA synthesis in proliferating trophoblast

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test → quantitative beta-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound**; ultrasound regardless of hCG when symptomatic
Extrauterine yolk sac/embryo diagnostic; adnexal mass/free fluid supportive; empty uterus alone insufficient
★ Stable pregnancy of unknown location → **repeat hCG in 48 hours**, serial ultrasound until resolved/localized
Discriminatory threshold up to 3,500 mIU/mL protects viable IUP; abnormal rise/fall cannot establish location

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/rupture concern → **IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent surgery**; do not await serial hCG
Confirmed unruptured, stable, reliable follow-up, low hCG, no fetal heartbeat → consider **methotrexate**
Avoid methotrexate: viable IUP, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal disease, cytopenias, immunodeficiency, unreliable follow-up
Postmethotrexate hCG days 4/7: fall ≥15% → weekly until negative; inadequate fall → reassess/re-dose/surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, death, tubal loss, recurrence, impaired fertility
Methotrexate: mucositis, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression; rupture remains possible despite falling hCG

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat/prevent STIs, smoking cessation; prior ectopic → early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancy
Methotrexate counseling: avoid alcohol, folate supplements, intercourse until resolution; avoid conception for 3 months
Unsensitized Rh-negative ectopic → Rh(D) immune globulin; provide return precautions for escalating pain/dizziness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Miscarriage: intrauterine pregnancy loss; passage of decidual tissue alone does not prove IUP
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: ovarian source, may coexist with normal pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary

table.title: Alternative definitive branches
rows: Stable, minimal symptoms, low declining hCG
Selected expectant management with reliable surveillance
Heartbeat, high hCG, or medical contraindication

ectopic-pregnancy.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG ectopic pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ectopic-pregnancy), [NICE tubal ectopic management](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG126/chapter/management-of-tubal-ectopic-pregnancy); conservative discriminatory threshold established ACOG teaching.

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → endoscopic septotomy/cricopharyngeal myotomy; avoid blind nasogastric instrumentation

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

esophageal-perforation.name: Esophageal perforation
esophageal-perforation.scope: Boerhaave syndrome, iatrogenic perforation, mediastinitis, gastrografin esophagography, emergent surgical repair
esophageal-perforation.core: Severe chest pain after vomiting or esophageal instrumentation, with systemic toxicity or mediastinal air, is an esophageal emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Endoscopy, dilation, foreign bodies, caustic injury; forceful emesis causes spontaneous Boerhaave rupture
Underlying stricture or malignancy increases instrumentation-related injury risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, fever, dyspnea, odynophagia; neck swelling or palpable crepitus
★ **Left pleural effusion**, pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema after retching
Hypotension, rising lactate, organ dysfunction → uncontrolled contamination and sepsis
Classic vomiting–pain–emphysema triad often incomplete; absence does not exclude rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Full-thickness tear releases saliva, gastric contents and bacteria into mediastinum/pleura
Boerhaave typically affects distal posterolateral esophagus; contamination causes chemical then infectious mediastinitis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable suspected leak → **CT chest with water-soluble oral contrast** or water-soluble esophagram
Gastrografin study negative with persistent suspicion → thin barium study to detect small leaks
Chest radiograph supportive only; normal early film does not rule out injury
Avoid routine diagnostic endoscopy when insufflation could enlarge an uncontained tear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO**, IV fluids, IV piperacillin–tazobactam, urgent thoracic/general surgery consultation
★ Free leak, shock or extensive contamination → **urgent repair and drainage**
Contained leak without sepsis → monitored antibiotics, nutritional support, drainage ± endoscopic closure/stent
IV proton-pump inhibitor; enteral feeding distal to leak or parenteral nutrition
Avoid blind nasogastric placement; decompression, if needed, under specialist guidance

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, empyema, septic shock, multiorgan failure; delay markedly worsens outcomes
Persistent fistula, esophageal stricture and malnutrition after healing

rows.label: Prevention
items: Careful procedural technique; prompt evaluation of new pain following esophageal instrumentation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mallory–Weiss: mucosal tear causing hematemesis without mediastinal contamination
ACS: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern; no contrast leak
Acute aortic syndrome: vascular abnormality on CT angiography

esophageal-perforation.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency esophageal management.

extremity-vascular-injury.name: Extremity vascular injury
extremity-vascular-injury.scope: Hard signs (pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, absent pulses, thrill/bruit, pallor), soft signs (diminished pulse, proximity), surgical exploration vs CT angiography
extremity-vascular-injury.core: After limb trauma, active arterial bleeding or threatened perfusion requires immediate intervention; stable equivocal findings require objective vascular assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Penetrating wounds near major vessels; blunt crush or traction injury
Knee dislocation, supracondylar humeral fracture, open fractures; spontaneous joint reduction may conceal mechanism

rows.label: Clues
items: Pain, pallor, coolness, paresthesia, paralysis indicate worsening ischemia; motor deficit is late
★ **Normal distal pulses do not exclude injury**, especially intimal tears after knee dislocation
Examine both limbs and document pulses, motor function, sensation before and after reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transection causes hemorrhage; intimal disruption → thrombosis and delayed ischemia
Contained arterial leak → pseudoaneurysm; artery–vein communication → traumatic AV fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hard signs → immediate **operative exploration**; imaging must not delay limb-saving treatment
Stable without hard signs → ABI/API; **<0.9** or abnormal examination → CT angiography
Normal examination + index ≥0.9 → serial examinations/follow-up; observe high-risk blunt injuries
Duplex ultrasound alternative in selected stable patients; CTA localizes injury for repair

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Direct pressure; uncontrolled hemorrhage → proximal tourniquet; avoid blind clamping
Resuscitate hemorrhagic shock with blood products; urgent vascular surgery consultation
★ Restore arterial flow rapidly, ideally within 6 hours; primary repair or vein graft
Temporary shunt when definitive repair delayed; coordinate fracture stabilization and revascularization
Prolonged ischemia, crush injury, marked swelling → early fasciotomy; monitor reperfusion hyperkalemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Amputation, persistent neuropathy, compartment syndrome; rhabdomyolysis and AKI after reperfusion
Delayed thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, graft infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Repeat neurovascular checks after splinting, reduction, and repair; promptly loosen constrictive dressings
Discharge follow-up essential for delayed swelling, recurrent bleeding, bruit, or new ischemic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Compartment syndrome: pain with passive stretch, tense compartments; pulses often remain palpable
Isolated nerve injury: focal deficits without objective perfusion abnormality

table.title: Trauma signs
rows: Absent pulses; bruit/thrill; overt distal ischemia
Diminished pulse; stable hematoma; prior bleeding

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency; elevated BUN/creatinine ratio supports upper source

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Active exsanguination → blood immediately regardless of hemoglobin; cardiac ischemia → individualize higher threshold
Severe life-threatening anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; persistent bleeding after endoscopy → IR/surgery
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention or perineal hematoma → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Renal concern, stable → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images; microscopic hematuria plus hypotension qualifies
Normal hematuria assessment cannot exclude renal vascular injury after high-energy deceleration
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; high clinical suspicion should not delay exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect elevation → age/gestation/risk-based phototherapy; exchange transfusion at critical thresholds
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypoglycemia.name: Hypoglycemia
hypoglycemia.scope: Drug-induced hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), Whipple triad, acute management (dextrose, glucagon), insulinoma
hypoglycemia.core: Compatible symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief with correction establish Whipple triad and justify evaluation for a hypoglycemic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Insulin, sulfonylureas; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney failure increase risk
Sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency; insulinoma causes fasting episodes in otherwise well adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Adrenergic: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger; neuroglycopenic: confusion, visual change, seizures, coma
Autonomic neuropathy or recurrent episodes may blunt warning symptoms
★ Glucose **<54 mg/dL** clinically significant; diabetes alert threshold <70 mg/dL

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess insulin suppresses glucose output and ketones; substrate/hormone deficits impair counterregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; plasma confirmation if discordant, never delay emergency correction
Critical sample: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen
Suspected endogenous fasting disorder → supervised fast up to 72 h; mixed-meal test for postprandial symptoms
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma → pancreatic CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound if localization unclear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Awake and swallowing → **15 g rapid carbohydrate**, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if needed
★ Altered or unable to swallow → **IV dextrose**; no IV access → IM/intranasal glucagon
After recovery → longer-acting carbohydrate; glucagon less effective after alcohol or glycogen depletion
★ Sulfonylurea recurrence → **octreotide + dextrose**, prolonged observation; long-acting insulin may require infusion
Adjust diabetes regimen and treat trigger; localized insulinoma → surgical resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Seizures, brain injury, arrhythmias, falls; recurrent episodes cause impaired awareness
Dextrose alone after sulfonylurea exposure may stimulate further insulin release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Meal/exercise planning, glucose monitoring or CGM alarms, caregiver rescue-glucagon education
Relax overly intensive targets when recurrent events, frailty, or impaired awareness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic attack: normal glucose during symptoms
Stroke: focal deficit may persist after glucose correction; evaluate both if unresolved

hypoglycemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine diagnostic and hypoglycemia treatment principles.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum; PSC particularly associated with UC
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention suggests **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Steroids induce remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas, strictures, obstruction and B12 deficiency in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

inguinal-hernia.name: Inguinal hernia
inguinal-hernia.scope: Direct inguinal hernia, indirect inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, incarcerated and strangulated hernia, physical exam, elective vs emergent surgical repair
inguinal-hernia.core: A groin bulge enlarging with strain suggests hernia; a painful irreducible mass with obstructive or ischemic signs requires urgent surgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Male sex, family history, prematurity, persistent processus vaginalis
Age-related fascial weakness, chronic cough, constipation, heavy strain; femoral hernias more frequent in women

rows.label: Clues
items: Bulge or dragging discomfort with standing/Valsalva, improving supine or after reduction
Incarcerated: contents cannot be reduced; bowel obstruction causes vomiting, distention, obstipation
★ **Severe persistent pain**, tenderness, erythema, toxicity/peritonitis → impaired perfusion; fever may be late

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abdominal contents protrude through a weak opening; a narrow neck impairs venous then arterial perfusion
Richter hernia traps only bowel-wall segment; ischemia may occur without complete obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Standing groin examination with cough/Valsalva**; inspect both sides and assess reducibility
Uncertain occult lesion → dynamic ultrasound; CT if obstruction, complication, or alternative diagnosis suspected
Clinical strangulation → immediate operation; imaging must not delay treatment
Do not rely on surface examination alone to reliably distinguish direct from indirect anatomy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Strangulation → **IV fluids, NPO, analgesia, antibiotics, emergency repair**; resect nonviable bowel
Incarceration without ischemic features → urgent surgeon evaluation; gentle reduction only in selected cases
★ Symptomatic inguinal hernia → **elective mesh repair** in adults; children → herniotomy
Minimally symptomatic men may choose watchful waiting with return precautions
Women and femoral hernias → timely repair because occult femoral disease and strangulation risk are greater

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel obstruction, ischemic necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Repair → chronic groin pain, recurrence, wound/mesh infection, testicular ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and chronic cough, smoking cessation, weight management; risk reduction cannot close an existing defect
After reduction or observation: urgent return for escalating pain, vomiting, or loss of reducibility

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphadenopathy: discrete solid nodes without cough impulse
Hydrocele: transilluminates; confined fluid rather than reducible bowel
Saphena varix: compressible venous swelling; Doppler demonstrates venous flow

table.title: Anatomic distinctions
rows: Below inguinal ligament, medial femoral vein

inherited-thrombophilias.name: Inherited thrombophilias
inherited-thrombophilias.scope: Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance), prothrombin G20210A mutation, protein C and protein S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, venous thromboembolism, pregnancy complications, anticoagulation management
inherited-thrombophilias.core: Inherited procoagulant states predispose chiefly to venous thrombosis; testing matters only when results change prevention or treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: First-degree relative with high-risk thrombophilia, young/recurrent VTE, unusual venous site
Pregnancy, estrogen, surgery, immobilization amplify risk; homozygous/combined defects are higher risk

rows.label: Clues
items: DVT, pulmonary embolism; family clustering supports inherited predisposition but may be absent
★ **Heparin resistance** suggests antithrombin deficiency; neonatal purpura fulminans suggests severe protein C deficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess clotting activity or deficient natural anticoagulants shifts hemostasis toward thrombin generation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm suspected VTE with **compression ultrasound** or pulmonary imaging before etiologic testing
Factor V/prothrombin DNA assays unaffected by acute thrombosis; functional assays often unreliable during acute illness
Pregnancy/estrogen lowers protein S; warfarin lowers C/S; heparin and acute clotting alter antithrombin
Defer functional testing until confounders resolved; do not stop necessary anticoagulation simply to test
No routine panel for isolated miscarriage, preeclampsia, FGR, or asymptomatic general population; MTHFR testing unhelpful

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute pregnancy VTE → **therapeutic LMWH**; UFH when rapid reversibility needed
Nonpregnant VTE → DOAC or warfarin; duration depends on provocation, recurrence, bleeding risk
Pregnancy prophylaxis depends on prior VTE and specific/family risk; low-risk heterozygosity alone often needs surveillance
★ Prior unprovoked/estrogen-related VTE generally warrants antepartum prophylaxis; prior VTE → postpartum prophylaxis
Protein C/S deficiency: overlap heparin when starting warfarin; avoid unopposed loading

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent embolism, post-thrombotic syndrome; anticoagulants → bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Inherited thrombophilia does not establish causation for pregnancy loss; empiric heparin does not improve unexplained loss

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **estrogen-containing contraception** in high-risk thrombophilia/VTE; prophylaxis during major transient risks

rows.label: Mimics
items: APS: acquired antibodies, arterial events and characteristic obstetric morbidity
Cancer-associated thrombosis: acquired hypercoagulability with systemic/malignancy findings

inherited-thrombophilias.evidence: Pregnancy prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [ASH teaching guidance](https://www.hematology.org/-/media/hematology/files/clinicians/guidelines/vte/ash-teaching-slide-setvtepregnancypdffinal71923.pdf); remaining content established hematology.

intussusception.name: Intussusception
intussusception.scope: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, pathologic lead points (Meckel, polyp), target sign on ultrasound, air enema
intussusception.core: Bowel telescoping causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia, often in a previously healthy infant with episodic distress and deceptively well intervals.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age 6–36 months; lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness
Older child, recurrent episode or adult → pathologic lead point: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Sudden recurrent **colicky pain with knees drawn up**, pallor and vomiting
Lethargy can dominate; bilious emesis or distention suggests progressing obstruction
Sausage-shaped RUQ mass, empty RLQ; currant-jelly stool is late and often absent
Shock, guarding, fever or peritonitis → compromised bowel/perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Proximal bowel and mesentery invaginate distally → venous congestion, edema and arterial ischemia
Ileocolic location most common in children; bleeding reflects injured mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound first** → target/doughnut on transverse view, pseudokidney longitudinally
Plain radiograph for obstruction/free air when severe findings; normal radiograph does not exclude
CT generally for adult cases or uncertain alternative diagnosis, not routine pediatric first test
Classic clinical triad uncommon; do not delay testing until bloody stools appear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV fluids**, analgesia; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Stable without peritonitis/perforation → **air or contrast enema reduction** with surgical backup
Failed reduction, perforation, shock or peritonitis → urgent surgery; resect nonviable bowel
Persistent/recurrent disease or suspected lead point → surgical evaluation; adult cases usually require resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, shock; recurrence after successful reduction
Enema-associated perforation → immediate surgical management

rows.label: Prevention
items: No usual primary prevention for idiopathic disease; remove identified pathologic lead point
After reduction → observe recovery, resume intake when tolerated; counsel on recurrent episodic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea predominates, less discrete symptom-free intervals
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate, urgent surgical evaluation

malignant-hyperthermia.name: Malignant hyperthermia
malignant-hyperthermia.scope: Ryanodine receptor (RYR1) mutation, trigger agents (succinylcholine, volatile anesthetics), masseter spasm, rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, IV dantrolene
malignant-hyperthermia.core: Unexpected intraoperative hypercapnia and rigidity after triggering anesthesia: stop exposure and give dantrolene before waiting for fever.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics**, e.g., sevoflurane; previous safe exposure does not exclude susceptibility
Autosomal dominant predisposition; personal/family anesthetic reaction, certain congenital myopathies

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Rapidly rising **end-tidal CO2 despite ventilation**, tachycardia, masseter spasm, generalized rigidity
Mixed respiratory/metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, dark urine, markedly elevated CK
Hyperthermia may be late; arrhythmias or cardiovascular collapse indicate severe disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: **RYR1** dysfunction → uncontrolled sarcoplasmic-reticulum Ca release in skeletal muscle
Sustained contraction consumes ATP and oxygen → CO2, heat, acidosis, muscle breakdown

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** during crisis; do not delay treatment for laboratory confirmation
ABG, electrolytes, CK, urine myoglobin, coagulation studies track severity
After recovery: caffeine–halothane muscle contracture testing; genetic testing supports family evaluation
Negative genetic panel does not exclude susceptibility; document anesthetic record and exposure timing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stop triggers; call for help; ventilate **100% oxygen** at high flow
★ **Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV**, repeat until hypermetabolism controlled; continue maintenance to prevent recurrence
Active cooling for marked hyperthermia; stop near 38 °C; IV fluids and urine-output monitoring
Treat hyperkalemia with insulin/dextrose; correct severe acidosis; avoid verapamil/diltiazem with dantrolene
ICU monitoring ≥24 hours; serial temperature, CO2, potassium, CK, renal function, coagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis → AKI; hyperkalemic arrhythmia, DIC, multiorgan failure
Recrudescence after initial control; dantrolene-associated muscle weakness and respiratory compromise

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medical alert identification; inform relatives and anesthesia teams before future procedures
Trigger-free anesthesia: propofol, local anesthetics, nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers; prepare anesthesia machine
Facilities using trigger agents require immediately accessible dantrolene and a crisis protocol

rows.label: Mimics
items: NMS: dopamine antagonist exposure; evolves over hours to days
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus and hyperreflexia
Inadequate ventilation: elevated CO2 without generalized rigidity or rhabdomyolysis

neck-trauma.name: Neck trauma
neck-trauma.scope: Penetrating neck trauma, zone I-III neck injuries, blunt vascular injury, hard vs soft signs of vascular injury
neck-trauma.core: Airway and hemorrhage take priority in neck injury; physiology and examination guide intervention more than the wound’s anatomic zone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Stab/gunshot wounds penetrating platysma; high-energy blunt trauma, hanging, cervical hyperextension
Cervical spine fractures, basilar skull fracture or neck seat-belt injury with concerning findings → vascular-injury risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hard signs**: pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, bruit/thrill, shock or focal neurologic deficit
Airway compromise: stridor, major air leak, rapidly increasing swelling; possible occult laryngotracheal injury
Soft signs: minor hemoptysis, dysphagia, nonexpanding hematoma, historical bleeding; stable findings still require evaluation
Delayed stroke, headache or partial Horner syndrome may follow blunt carotid dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Arterial laceration/dissection causes hemorrhage, thromboembolism or stroke
Aerodigestive disruption permits obstruction, contamination and mediastinal infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable penetrating injury with soft signs/concerning trajectory → **CT angiography** of neck
Suspected esophageal injury → contrast esophagram and/or endoscopy; negative CTA alone may miss small perforation
Suspected laryngotracheal injury → flexible laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy; assess cervical spine in blunt trauma
Blunt cerebrovascular screening → CTA according to injury pattern and neurologic findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/hard signs → **airway control and immediate operative exploration**, no imaging delay
Direct pressure for hemorrhage, blood-product resuscitation; avoid blind clamping/probing
Threatened distorted airway → expert intubation with surgical-airway backup; avoid repeated traumatic attempts
★ Stable blunt dissection → **antiplatelet or anticoagulation** when bleeding risk permits; vascular consultation
Esophageal perforation → NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent source control

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, airway loss, exsanguination; pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, mediastinitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Spinal motion restriction for suspected cervical injury; restraints and violence-risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Superficial wound: platysma intact; still examine surrounding structures
Isolated soft-tissue hematoma: no vascular/aerodigestive lesion after evaluation

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.name: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.scope: COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition mechanism, renal adverse effects (sodium retention, acute kidney injury), gastrointestinal toxicity, cardiovascular risks
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.core: NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever through cyclooxygenase inhibition, with gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular tradeoffs.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Pain, dysmenorrhea, renal colic, gout; **lowest effective dose, shortest duration**
Topical diclofenac for localized joint pain reduces systemic exposure

rows.label: Mechanism
items: COX-1: gastric/platelet/renal effects; COX-2: inflammatory prostaglandins and endothelial prostacyclin
Most reversibly inhibit enzymes; aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ **Afferent arteriolar constriction** → AKI, hyperkalemia, sodium retention, hypertension/HF worsening
★ Gastritis, **ulcer/bleeding**; platelet inhibition except with selective COX-2 agents
MI/stroke risk; interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy; bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma

rows.label: Avoid
items: Active GI bleeding, severe CKD, decompensated HF, peri-CABG setting
Pregnancy ≥20 weeks generally avoid; later gestation → ductal closure and fetal renal injury
Aspirin in children with viral illness → Reye syndrome

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID → **high AKI risk**
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets → bleeding; NSAIDs can increase lithium and methotrexate exposure

rows.label: Monitor
items: BP, edema, creatinine, K; assess melena/anemia and prior ulcer history
High GI risk → consider PPI; reassess need rather than automatically continuing indefinitely

rows.label: Traps
items: Celecoxib reduces GI/platelet effects but retains renal and thrombotic risks
Prescribed low-dose aspirin for obstetric indications remains an exception to pregnancy NSAID restriction
Do not combine multiple NSAIDs for additional analgesia

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.evidence: Pregnancy safety checked 2026-10-30: [FDA NSAID warning](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-recommends-avoiding-use-nsaids-pregnancy-20-weeks-or-later-because-they-can-result-low-amniotic); other pharmacology: established teaching.

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascites, fixed irregular pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion or bowel obstruction
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
